Extract matches of dependency patterns from texts using spaCy

Source: R/spacy_extract_dependency_matches.R
spacy_extract_dependency_matches.Rd

Find tokens that are connected in the dependency parse in the way a pattern describes, using spaCy's DependencyMatcher (see https://spacy.io/usage/rule-based-matching#dependencymatcher). Where spacy_extract_matches() finds sequences of adjacent tokens, a dependency pattern finds tokens by their relations, wherever they are in the sentence, and returns each of them: the verb of a passive clause together with its subject and its agent, for instance.

Usage

spacy_extract_dependency_matches(
  x,
  patterns,
  n_process = 1L,
  batch_size = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

a character object or a TIF-compliant corpus data.frame (see https://github.com/ropensci/tif)

patterns

a named list of dependency patterns in spaCy's structure, in which each name is the label of a pattern. A pattern is a list of nodes, each a named list that describes one token:

  • RIGHT_ID: a name for the node, which labels the token it matches in the output;

  • RIGHT_ATTRS: the attributes of the token, as for a token of spacy_extract_matches(), such as list(DEP = "nsubjpass"); an empty list() matches any token;

  • LEFT_ID and REL_OP, for every node but the first: the name of an earlier node, and the operator that relates that node to this one, such as ">" when this node is a direct dependent of the earlier one.

The names must be unique, and each label has one pattern: give alternative patterns labels of their own.

n_process

the number of processes for spaCy's nlp.pipe() to use: 1 (the default) processes the documents in the current R session's Python process, a larger number starts that many Python processes, and -1 uses all CPUs. Starting the processes and loading the model in each takes time, so more than one process helps only for large numbers of documents. A custom pipeline component must be defined in an importable Python module to be used in other processes.

batch_size

the number of documents that spaCy's nlp.pipe() processes together; NULL (the default) uses the pipeline's default (nlp.batch_size). Larger batches can be faster, but use more memory.

...

unused

Value

A data.frame with one row for each node of the pattern in each match, and no rows when nothing matches. Two nodes of a pattern can match the same token, which then has a row for each:

doc_id

the document

match_id

the number of the match within the document, starting at 1 in each document, so that doc_id and match_id together identify a match

label

the label of the pattern

node

the name of the node that the token matched, from RIGHT_ID

sentence_id, token_id

the sentence of the token that the node matched, and its position in that sentence, both starting at 1 as in spacy_parse()

start_id

the position of the token in the document, starting at 1

token

the text of the token

Rows are in the order of the documents in x. Within a document, matches are ordered by the positions of their tokens, taken in the order of the pattern's nodes (so first by the token of the first node), then by the order of the labels in patterns; match_id numbers them in that order. The rows of a match are in the order of the nodes.

Details

The operators in REL_OP are spaCy's: among others, "A > B" when B is a direct dependent of A, "A < B" when B is the head of A, "A >> B" when B is anywhere below A, and "A . B" when B directly follows A. See the link above for all of them.

The pipeline needs a dependency parser, or another component that sets dependencies: a pattern that relates nodes gives an error for a document that has no dependency parse, rather than no matches. The labels of dependency relations and tags differ between language models; spacy_parse(x, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE) shows those of the model in use. A match is only as good as the model's parse of the text.

A pattern can match many times in a sentence: a verb and any one of its dependents gives one match for each dependent. Patterns that ask for an entity type (ENT_TYPE or ENT_IOB) give a warning when no component sets entities, since they then match nothing.

See also

spacy_extract_matches() for sequences of adjacent tokens.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
spacy_initialize()

txt <- c(doc1 = "The book was written by Jane. Jane wrote the book.",
         doc2 = "Mistakes were made, and the report is being rewritten.")

# passive clauses, by the labels of the English models: a past participle
# with a passive subject and a passive auxiliary as its dependents
passive <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "verb", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "subject",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "nsubjpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass"))
)
# the same, with the agent: "by" and its object
agent <- c(passive, list(
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "by",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "agent")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "by", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "agent",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "pobj"))
))
m <- spacy_extract_dependency_matches(txt, list(PASSIVE = passive,
                                                PASSIVE_AGENT = agent))
m

# one row for each match, with a column for each node
reshape(m[m$label == "PASSIVE", c("doc_id", "match_id", "node", "token")],
        idvar = c("doc_id", "match_id"), timevar = "node",
        direction = "wide")
} # }
